strengths: Principled adaptation of Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) to language modeling: Replacing full model replication or bulky output classification heads with parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) is computationally clever, structurally sound, and well-suited for modern LLMs.

Solid theoretical foundation and toy validation: Connecting the WTA loss to conditional hard-EM, deriving theoretical bounds on achievable entropy, and demonstrating the mode-splitting behavior on a mixture of Markov chains provides clear insight into why standard MLE averages modes while LoRA-MCL isolates them.

Rigorous large-scale empirical evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly evaluated on modern large multimodal models (Qwen2-Audio 8.4B and LLaVA-1.6 7B) across multiple domains (audio captioning on Clotho-V2 and AudioCaps, vision-language captioning on TextCaps) with well-calibrated parameter- and compute-matched baselines.

Convincing validation of hypothesis specialization: The controlled bilingual experiment (Section 5.3.2) provides direct qualitative and quantitative confirmation that distinct LoRA heads actively specialize to different modes (English vs. French) rather than collapsing.
weaknesses: Reliance on oracle evaluation metrics: The quantitative generation quality metrics (e.g., SPIDEr, CIDEr, BLEU-4) are computed using sentence-based oracle evaluation (best-of-K against ground truth). While standard in MCL literature, this naturally rewards high diversity when multiple reference annotations exist, and leaves open the question of how a downstream application or user selects a final hypothesis without access to ground truth.

Activation and computational overhead during training: Duplicating the input $K$ times along the batch dimension to execute parallel LoRA branches via group convolution scales the intermediate activation memory and attention computation by $O(K)$, which limits scalability to larger numbers of hypotheses ($K$) or long-context tasks.

Hyperparameter sensitivity of the WTA relaxation: The relaxed WTA loss relies on an $\varepsilon$ smoothing parameter to avoid adapter collapse, but performance and diversity are sensitive to this choice (as visible in Tables 5–6), requiring task-specific tuning without a general dynamic annealing schedule integrated into the main pipeline.

Lack of learned mixture weights at inference: The framework outputs $K$ unconditional hypotheses without producing calibrated posterior probabilities or ranking scores $p(z_k | c)$ for each adapter, making hypothesis selection ambiguous when a single output is required.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated adaptation of Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) to language models via Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA-MCL), neatly circumventing the prohibitive parameter overhead of multi-head LM projections.

Solid theoretical framing connecting the Winner-Takes-All (WTA) objective to a conditional hard-EM algorithm, with clear information-theoretic bounds and analytical characterization on mixtures of Markov chains.

Comprehensive empirical validation on large open foundation models (Qwen2-Audio 8.4B and LLaVA-1.6 7B) across audio captioning and visual captioning, demonstrating a superior quality-diversity trade-off over competitive Diverse Beam Search baselines.
The controlled bilingual experiment (Section 5.3.2) and the synthetic Markov chain simulations provide compelling, transparent empirical validation of hypothesis specialization.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies heavily on oracle metrics across the K hypotheses (selecting the best candidate against ground truth); however, in practical deployment where a single output or ranked outputs are needed, LoRA-MCL lacks a mechanism to estimate the prior mode distribution p(z_k | c) without extra scoring modules.

Duplicating representations by K along the effective batch dimension incurs a non-trivial memory and compute overhead in self-attention activation memory (scaling with K x b x T x d), but the paper lacks explicit reporting of wall-clock training throughput and peak VRAM consumption.
The method requires careful tuning of the relaxation parameter epsilon to balance hypothesis collapse against homogenization, and an automatic or annealed scheduling mechanism is left to future work.

The empirical evaluation is restricted to captioning domains (audio and vision-language); validating the method on purely textual ambiguous tasks (e.g., diverse dialogue or story continuation) would further establish generality.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and elegant framework (LoRA-MCL) that adapts the Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) paradigm to language model fine-tuning by leveraging multiple LoRA adapters instead of parameter-heavy prediction heads.

The theoretical framing is sound and insightful: it connects Winner-Takes-All (WTA) training to conditional hard-EM, derives theoretical lower and upper bounds for optimal achievable loss on mixture distributions, and demonstrates both analytically and empirically how standard MLE averages modes on Markov chains while MCL recovers them.

The engineering design is efficient and practical, proposing a parallelized grouped convolution implementation that computes adapter forward passes across all hypotheses in a single batch without sequential looping.

Comprehensive experimental validation on large multimodal foundation models (Qwen2-Audio 8.4B and LLaVA-1.6 7B) across audio and visual captioning benchmarks (Clotho-V2, AudioCaps, TextCaps), demonstrating an attractive diversity-quality Pareto frontier compared to Diverse Beam Search and Beam Search baselines under matching parameter budgets.
The bilingual captioning experiment provides a compelling, intuitive demonstration of hypothesis specialization, confirming that distinct adapters isolate distinct distributional modes.
weaknesses: Inference candidate selection is not addressed: evaluation relies on oracle scoring against ground-truth references. In realistic downstream applications where reference captions are unavailable, selecting the most appropriate hypothesis among the $K$ generated candidates remains an open question, as the current model does not train a routing or scoring head.

Mixed results on stochastic decoding: the empirical gains of LoRA-MCL over LoRA-MLE with sampling-based decoding (Tables 7 and 8) are modest and inconsistent across metrics, suggesting that the primary advantage of MCL manifests mainly under deterministic/MAP search rather than standard nucleus or typical sampling.

Computational overhead during training: duplicating the hidden representations $K$ times along the batch dimension ($bK \times T \times d$) increases activation memory and computation. A clearer discussion of actual wall-clock training times and memory scaling compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning would strengthen the submission.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: the relaxed WTA weighting parameter $\epsilon$ requires careful manual tuning to balance mode collapse prevention against hypothesis homogenization, though the authors candidly acknowledge this limitation.

strengths: Principled adaptation of Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) to autoregressive language modeling using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), providing an effective and parameter-efficient alternative to multi-head or full-ensemble methods for handling multimodal output distributions.

Solid theoretical backing linking the training objective to conditional hard-EM and deriving information-theoretic loss bounds, nicely supported by an analytical derivation and synthetic verification on mixtures of Markov chains.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains and modalities (audio captioning on AudioCaps and Clotho, image captioning on TextCaps, and machine translation on WMT/Flores) using strong base models (Qwen2-Audio-8B, LLaVA-1.6-7B, ALMA-7B).

Thorough benchmarking against competitive baselines, including parameter-matched LoRA-MLE, LoRA-MoE, Diverse Beam Search (DBS), Test-Time Augmentation (TTA), and task-specific diffusion baselines (DAC-RLD).
Compelling analysis of hypothesis specialization, evidenced both qualitatively and quantitatively via a controlled bilingual setup and SVM classification over candidate embeddings.
weaknesses: Evaluation heavily relies on oracle NLG metrics (taking the best candidate among K against references), which naturally benefits multi-hypothesis approaches over single-mode generation; human evaluation or downstream utility assessment would provide clearer validation of real-world plausibility.

The number of hypotheses K is static across all inputs, whereas natural contexts exhibit varying degrees of ambiguity—some prompts are unimodal while others have many modes, potentially forcing unnecessary divergence or redundant heads.

Although the grouped convolution implementation removes sequential forward loops, replicating intermediate activations K times along the batch dimension still scales memory footprint and computation linearly with K during training.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: Adapting Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) via multiple Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA-MCL) rather than output heads provides an elegant, scalable, and parameter-efficient solution for modeling multi-modal distributions in large auto-regressive models.

Efficient implementation: The use of grouped 1D convolutions to compute the K adapter hypotheses in parallel over a single frozen backbone cleverly circumvents the linear runtime penalty of naive multi-hypothesis training.

Solid theoretical foundation: The manuscript provides a rigorous link between the Winner-Takes-All objective and conditional hard-EM, establishes informative upper and lower entropy bounds, and validates the theoretical mechanics cleanly on synthetic Markov chain mixtures.

Thorough and broad empirical evaluation: The method is validated across three distinct multimodal and text-generation domains (audio captioning with Qwen2-Audio, vision-language captioning with LLaVA, and machine translation with ALMA-7B), consistently demonstrating favorable quality–diversity trade-offs against competitive baselines (e.g., Diverse Beam Search, LoRA-MoE, and test-time augmentation).

Insightful analysis of hypothesis specialization: The bilingual image captioning experiment and linear SVM classification on generated sentence embeddings offer clear, quantitative evidence that the adapters genuinely specialize into distinct semantic modes rather than collapsing.
weaknesses: Reliance on oracle evaluation metrics: Because the evaluation uses oracle metrics (taking the maximum metric across the K hypotheses against ground-truth references), candidate generation is well rewarded for spread. While standard in MCL literature, the manuscript does not provide an inference-time mechanism or scoring function to rank/select the best candidate when ground-truth references are unavailable.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Performance is sensitive to the choice of the relaxation parameter epsilon or annealing schedule parameters (as shown in Table 5), where slight misconfigurations can lead to either mode collapse or over-homogenization toward standard MLE behavior.

Limited exploration of scaling K: The experiments primarily focus on small K (K ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7}); the practical scalability and memory behavior for significantly larger numbers of modes/hypotheses remain unaddressed.

strengths: Principled adaptation of Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) to autoregressive generation: Leveraging multiple Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) neatly circumvents the severe memory and parameter bottlenecks of multi-head MCL caused by massive language model vocabulary heads (e.g., 640M parameters for Qwen2-Audio's lm_head).

Solid theoretical and synthetic grounding: The authors formally connect LoRA-MCL to conditional hard-EM, derive lower and upper bounds on optimal WTA loss under mixture assumptions, and theoretically and empirically demonstrate on Markov chain mixtures that MLE averages modes while MCL separates them.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse domains: The method is evaluated on audio captioning (Clotho-V2, AudioCaps with Qwen2-Audio 8.4B), vision-language captioning (TextCaps with LLaVA-1.6 7.1B), and diverse machine translation (ALMA-7B). Strong baselines are included, such as parameter-matched LoRA-MLE, LoRA-MoE, Diverse Beam Search (DBS), Test-Time Augmentation (TTA), and task-specific models (DAC-RLD).

Convincing analysis of hypothesis specialization: The controlled bilingual experiment (translating half of TextCaps captions into French) clearly validates that hypotheses cleanly partition the data distribution modes (achieving 99.8% linear SVM classification accuracy between heads), complemented by PCA visualizations and non-synthetic SVM probe results on AudioCaps (63.7% vs. ~20% for baselines).

Efficient training implementation: Processing K adapter candidates simultaneously via grouped 1D convolutions (nn.Conv1d with K groups) avoids sequential looping and enables scalable batched training.
weaknesses: Reliance on oracle evaluation metrics: The reported quality gains rely on sentence-based oracle evaluation (max over K hypotheses against references) or Leave-One-Out BLEU. While standard in the MCL literature, practical downstream deployment often requires selecting a single best continuation or presenting scored candidates. The framework lacks a learned scoring head or prior estimator p(z_k | c), leaving candidate ranking unaddressed.

Marginal benefits under sampling-based decoding: When evaluated with stochastic sampling (Top-k, Nucleus, Typical p in Tables 9 and 11), LoRA-MCL yields only marginal improvements over standard LoRA-MLE, and slightly degrades quality metrics on Clotho. The distinct advantages appear primarily confined to MAP/beam search decoding.

Sensitivity to relaxation and annealing hyperparameters: Table 5 shows high sensitivity to the relaxation parameter ε and annealing decay rate ρ. If ε is moderately large (e.g., ≥0.1) or annealing is too slow, diversity rapidly collapses to the MLE regime, requiring careful task-specific tuning.

Fixed and small number of hypotheses K: The number of modes K is fixed in advance (K ∈ {3, 5, 7}) and kept small. The manuscript does not systematically explore behavior under mode misspecification (e.g., true multimodal distribution with many more modes than K, or K larger than true data modes).
